title: Section check: History & Human Stories
intro: 12 questions about Lessons 1–9. Take your time. You can look back at the lessons and try again as often as you like.

questions.question: The Riverstone drawing shows a river. The diary says traders came by boat. What do these two clues suggest together?

options.text: The river helped traders bring goods.
options.feedback: Yes. The drawing shows a river, and the diary talks about boats. Together, they suggest the river helped traders reach the market.

options.text: The market was quiet, with few people.
options.feedback: Not quite. These two clues are about the river and boats. The diary also says market day was crowded. Look back at Lesson 1.

options.text: Most traders came by cart, not boat.
options.feedback: Not quite. The drawing shows one cart, but the diary says traders came by boat. Look back at Lesson 1.

stimulus.title: A made-up source: a poster from the town of Norrin, about 40 years ago
items: On Saturday, in the town hall.

questions.question: A historian finds this poster. Which question needs a different source to answer?

options.text: Where was the book fair?
options.feedback: Not quite. The poster says the fair was in the town hall. So the poster can answer this. Look back at Lesson 1.

options.text: What time did story time start?
options.feedback: Not quite. The poster says story time was at 10:00. So the poster can answer this. Look back at Lesson 1.

options.text: How many people came to it?
options.feedback: Yes. The poster does not say how many people came. A historian would need another source, like a diary or a photo.

stimulus.title: A made-up object: a wooden spoon from the village of Tavi
items: One end is dark and burned.
There is a small crack in the handle.
A star is cut into the handle.

questions.question: Which sentence about the spoon is an inference?

options.text: The handle has a star cut into it.
options.feedback: Not quite. You can see the star on the handle, so this is an observation. Look back at Lesson 2.

options.text: It may have been used near a fire.
options.feedback: Yes. Nobody can see the fire now. You build this idea from a clue, the burned end. That makes it an inference.

options.text: There is a small crack in the handle.
options.feedback: Not quite. You can see the crack for yourself, so this is an observation. Look back at Lesson 2.

questions.question: What can a close view of the past show that a wide view may hide?

options.text: How a town grew over 100 years
options.feedback: Not quite. Growth over 100 years is a pattern. A wide view is good at showing patterns. Look back at Lesson 3.

options.text: One person's choices and feelings
options.feedback: Yes. A close view, like one diary, shows one person's choices and feelings. A wide view can hide people.

options.text: How a river moved over a long time
options.feedback: Not quite. A river that moves over hundreds of years is a pattern. A wide view shows this best. Look back at Lesson 3.

questions.question: Each kind of account answers its own kind of question. Which of these would a historian ask about an origin account?

options.text: How did the sun and the planets form?
options.feedback: Not quite. Scientists ask questions like this about nature. Historians ask who told an account, when and why. Look back at Lesson 4.

options.text: How should people live?
options.feedback: Not quite. Faith accounts and cultural accounts often answer questions like this. Historians ask who told an account, and why. Look back at Lesson 4.

options.text: Who told this account, and why?
options.feedback: Yes. Historians ask who told an account, when and why. Each kind of question needs its own kind of answer.

questions.question: A young person learns a skill from an older person. She makes it better. Then she teaches it to her friends. What is this called?

options.text: Collective learning
options.feedback: Yes. In collective learning, people share what they know, make it better and pass it on. This is how knowledge grows.

options.text: Trading with other groups
options.feedback: Not quite. Trade means you give something and get something back. Here, a skill is shared and made better. Look back at Lesson 5.

options.text: Foraging for wild food
options.feedback: Not quite. Foraging means finding wild food. This example is about sharing a skill and making it better. Look back at Lesson 5.

questions.question: Archaeologists found these clues at early human sites. Which clue could show what people cooked?

options.text: The handprints on a rock wall
options.feedback: Not quite. Handprints are a kind of art. They tell us other things, not what people cooked. Look back at Lesson 5.

options.text: The hearth with its burned seeds
options.feedback: Yes. A hearth is a place where people made a fire. Burned seeds in a hearth can show what people cooked.

options.text: Tools of the same shape, far apart
options.feedback: Not quite. These tools may show that people shared ideas. They do not show what people cooked. Look back at Lesson 5.

questions.question: After a good harvest, a farming village may have a surplus. What is a surplus?

options.text: More food than people need right now
options.feedback: Yes. A surplus is extra food. People can store it, so not everyone has to farm.

options.text: A plant that people grow for food
options.feedback: Not quite. A plant that people grow for food is a crop. A surplus is extra food or goods. Look back at Lesson 6.

options.text: Finding wild food instead of growing it
options.feedback: Not quite. Finding wild food is called foraging. A surplus is more food than people need right now. Look back at Lesson 6.

questions.question: Banwa is a made-up city. Many things change there over time. Which of these changes shows that some people gained more power than others?

options.text: Farms grow extra grain for several good years
options.feedback: Not quite. Extra grain helped Banwa grow. It does not show who has more power. Look back at Lesson 7.

options.text: People build a shared storehouse
options.feedback: Not quite. A shared storehouse shows people working together. It does not show who has more power. Look back at Lesson 7.

options.text: Some families control more land and grain
options.feedback: Yes. Families with more land and grain have more power. In early cities, power was not shared equally.

questions.question: In Babylon, King Hammurabi had rules carved on a tall stone. Everyone had to follow them. What are rules like these called?

options.text: Taxes
options.feedback: Not quite. A tax is something people give to their government, like grain or work. Look back at Lesson 7.

options.text: Laws
options.feedback: Yes. A law is a rule that everyone in a place must follow. Hammurabi had about 280 laws carved on a stone.

options.text: Goods
options.feedback: Not quite. Goods are things people make or grow, like jars or cloth. Look back at Lesson 7.

questions.question: Paper was first made in China. How did the idea of papermaking reach the Middle East and Europe?

options.text: It spread along the trade routes.
options.feedback: Yes. Traders carried ideas as well as goods. Papermaking spread along the routes to other lands.

options.text: Each place made it at the same time.
options.feedback: Not quite. Paper was first made in China. The idea reached other lands later. Look back at Lesson 8.

options.text: One trader took it on one long trip.
options.feedback: Not quite. The idea did not travel in one trip. It moved along trade routes, from place to place. Look back at Lesson 8.

stimulus.title: A made-up town: a new ticket machine
stimulus.body: The made-up town of Pellow puts a new ticket machine at its bus stop. Before, buying a ticket took 10 minutes. Now it takes one minute. But the screen shows words in only one language. It has no pictures to help.

questions.question: Who might find the new machine hard to use?

options.text: People who want to buy tickets quickly
options.feedback: Not quite. The machine is faster, so this is a benefit for these people. Look back at Lesson 9.

options.text: People who ride the bus every day
options.feedback: Not quite. People who ride often can save time every day. That is a benefit. Look back at Lesson 9.

options.text: People who cannot read that language
options.feedback: Yes. The screen uses only one language, so it is a barrier for some people. An invention only helps people who can use it.

results.high: Well done. You know a lot about how we learn about the past and how early communities changed.
results.middle: Good work. You got many questions right. Look back at the lessons for the ones you missed, and try again if you like.
results.low: Thank you for trying. Look back at Lessons 1–9, then try again. You can take as long as you need.
